bodyMarkdown:
## The idea in plain language

Walk all the way around the edge of a field and back to where you started, facing the same way. You have turned a full 360 degrees, no matter how many corners the field has — three or thirty.

That fact gives you the exterior angles instantly. Each interior angle is then just what is left over from a straight line.

## What is actually going on

Exterior angles of **any** polygon sum to 360. For a regular polygon with $n$ sides, each exterior angle is $\dfrac{360}{n}$, and each interior angle is its supplement.

Interior angles sum to $(n-2) \times 180$, because the polygon splits into $n - 2$ triangles.

For quadrilaterals, the family tree matters: a square is a rectangle **and** a rhombus; every rectangle is a parallelogram. Diagonals distinguish them — a rectangle's are equal, a rhombus's cross at right angles, a square's do both.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: Find each interior angle of a regular octagon.
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
Each exterior angle is $\dfrac{360}{8} = 45$ degrees.

Each interior angle is $180 - 45 = 135$ degrees.

Check: $8 \times 135 = 1080 = (8-2) \times 180$.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: How many diagonals does a decagon have?
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
Each of the 10 vertices connects to $10 - 3 = 7$ others by a diagonal (excluding itself and its two neighbours).

That counts $10 \times 7 = 70$, but each diagonal is counted from both ends.

Diagonals $= \dfrac{70}{2} = 35$.

formulaCards.title: Polygon angles
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: Interior angles sum to $(n-2) \times 180$. Exterior angles always sum to 360.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: A hexagon's interiors total 720; each is 120 if regular.

formulaCards.title: Diagonals
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: A polygon with $n$ sides has $\dfrac{n(n-3)}{2}$ diagonals.

formulaCards.title: Quadrilateral areas
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: Parallelogram: base $\times$ height. Trapezium: $\dfrac12(a+b)h$. Rhombus: $\dfrac12 d_1 d_2$.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: A rhombus with diagonals 6 and 8 has area 24.

commonTraps: Using $n \times 180$ for the interior sum instead of $(n-2) \times 180$.
Forgetting to halve when counting diagonals, so counting each one twice.
Assuming a parallelogram has equal diagonals. Only rectangles and squares do.
